provenance.sourceText: a signature, contract, or other record relating to such transaction may not be denied legal effect, validity, or enforceability solely because it is in electronic form; […] a contract relating to such transaction may not be denied legal effect, validity, or enforceability solely because an electronic signature or electronic record was used in its formation.

rules.notes: Electronic Signatures in Global and National Commerce Act ("E-SIGN Act"), 15 U.S.C. § 7001(a)(1)-(2), Pub. L. 106-229. Originally verified on 2026-08-30 via law.cornell.edu (Legal Information Institute's mirror). RE-VERIFIED live on 2026-09-01 directly against the official source itself: govinfo.gov (U.S. Government Publishing Office), https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2021-title15/html/USCODE-2021-title15-chap96-subchapI-sec7001.htm ("From the U.S. Government Publishing Office, www.gpo.gov") — the quoted text matches verbatim. uscode.house.gov (the House Office of the Law Revision Counsel's own site) was also attempted but timed out both times; govinfo.gov is an equally official, GPO-published source, not a secondary mirror. This is a GENERAL rule about electronic records/signatures, not a document-specific one, so it applies equally to a quote (not a tax document) — unlike FR's invoice.send rule, which is grounded in a tax-code article specific to invoices.

Recording a payment is an internal bookkeeping entry; no US text identified governing the act of declaring it in this tool. The resulting balance (paid/outstanding) is a projection shown on screen, never a document status — see invoice.descriptor.ts.

EN 16931 is a EUROPEAN TECHNICAL STANDARD (the socle of e-invoicing formats under EU Directive 2014/55/EU) — nothing found requiring a US company to produce or offer one; the US has no federal e-invoicing mandate at all (consistent with this same file's own notes elsewhere, and with country-identifiers/data/us.json's own EIN entry). Whether a normalized export should ever be REQUIRED for a US-based company is out of scope here on purpose — this ticket (item 12, "formats normalisés") only builds the FORMAT itself, never a legal claim about when it must be used; that question belongs to item 11 ("canal imposé par pays") or 15 ("mentions obligatoires"), neither of which this rule pretends to answer. This rule only allows the VOLUNTARY download of a normalized export (a product convenience, same category as 'export-accounting' below) — a US seller might still want to hand a European counterparty an EN 16931 document even with no domestic mandate of its own. No `statuses` here: the descriptor itself (invoice.descriptor.ts's own `availableWhen` on "download-xml") already restricts the action to already-numbered statuses (BT-1 has cardinality 1..1 in the standard) — a matching `statuses` here would be redundant, not a real extra country-policy restriction (see data/all.spec.ts's own guard against that). What would settle whether this should ever be mandatory: none of this standard's own scope names the US at all, so nothing to check here — only a hypothetical future US requirement would.

schemes.helpText: Employer Identification Number (optional for sole proprietors)

provenance.resolutionNote: This entry inherits the removed compliance engine's own choice (git tag avant-refonte-documents, backend/src/compliance/profiles/data/us.ts's requiredIdentifiers: scheme LEGAL_ID, label EIN, required false, 'optional for sole proprietors') — that profile carried NO provenance field at all, so the choice was never sourced there either. A live fetch of https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/employer-id-numbers on 2026-08-30 returned real IRS text: "You need an EIN if you: Have employees; Will need to pay employment, excise or alcohol, tobacco, and firearms taxes; Withhold taxes on income, other than wages, paid to a non-resident alien", and separately that partnerships, LLCs, corporations, tax-exempt organizations, estates, trusts, retirement plans/IRAs, REMICs and farmers' cooperatives must obtain one to operate at all. That page settles WHO must obtain an EIN to exist as a business — it does not settle whether an EIN must appear ON AN INVOICE, which is the actual claim this fact makes; the same fetch's own summary states plainly "the provided content does not address whether an EIN must appear on invoices." No US federal invoice-content mandate was found either (consistent with backend/src/modules/documents/country-policy/data/us.json's own notes on the absence of a federal e-invoicing mandate), so there is no separate invoice-content rule to point to. `required: false` is kept as the best-available default (a sole proprietor with no employees and none of the IRS triggers above genuinely has no EIN to put on anything) but is not itself sourced to a text about invoices. What would settle this: a source addressing invoice content specifically, e.g. a state's own invoicing/sales-tax-registration rules, since there is no federal one to check.

HEADLINE : il n'existe AUCUNE voie de correction de droit aux États-Unis, parce qu'il n'existe aucune facture de droit — 26 U.S.C. § 6001 impose des REGISTRES, pas un DOCUMENT, et l'IRS écrit que la loi n'exige aucun type de registre particulier. C'est un négatif ÉTABLI, pas une recherche qui a échoué. CAVEAT du YAML, porté tel quel : le négatif FÉDÉRAL est solide ; le négatif INFRA-NATIONAL ne l'est pas — seuls New York, la Californie et le Texas ont été vérifiés, et les 47 autres États n'ont pas été examinés sur la correction de facture (hors périmètre de C1 et de P3-T01 eux-mêmes, pas seulement de cette transcription).

provenance.resolutionNote: UPDATE (2026-09-01, item 21): a real attempt WAS made this time — this is no longer simply 'no research done'. California's own Revenue and Taxation Code § 6051 (read live via leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=6051.) states: 'a tax is hereby imposed upon all retailers at the rate of […] 4 3/4 percent thereafter' — NOT 7.25 as this fact encodes for CA. This is not a contradiction to silently fix: California's actual statewide combined rate is layered across SEVERAL separate statutory provisions this pass did not fully trace (the state General Fund rate under § 6051 and its own amending sections, plus the Bradley-Burns Uniform Local Sales and Use Tax under a different part of the Revenue and Taxation Code, plus at least one additional state-level fraction enacted after 1991) — no SINGLE provision states '7.25%' as a unified current figure the way CGI art. 278 states '20%' for France. The other five states' primary sources were fetched (NY Consolidated Laws via nysenate.gov, Texas Tax Code via statutes.capitol.texas.gov, Washington RCW via apps.leg.wa.gov all returned HTTP 200; Florida's leg.state.fl.us and Illinois's ilga.gov did not load in time) but were not read closely enough to confirm or refute their own encoded figures against a specific section, for the same reason: a US state sales tax rate is characteristically a STACK of state + county + city + special-district rates, not a fact one statute settles alone the way a VAT rate is. This whole catalog remains `unverified`, now for a demonstrated reason rather than an unstarted one. What would settle this: either reading every layered provision per state (a much larger undertaking than this pass, and one that would still go stale as rates change), or — as already suggested — wiring a real US sales-tax rate lookup API instead of a hand-typed table.
